intros.market: Five CAs control 91% of issuance volume, led by Internet Security Research Group at 36% and Google Trust Services at 21%. The CR3 concentration ratio stands at 74%, while 89 total CAs hold trust store positions. The HHI of 2189 indicates moderate concentration, though 75 CAs operate in the long tail with minimal market presence but full trust privileges.
intros.trust: The WebPKI operates with 335 trusted roots across four major trust stores, but only 90 roots appear in all four stores and just 38 CA owners achieve universal trust. Microsoft maintains 142 roots not present in Chrome, Mozilla, or Apple, creating operational complexity where certificate chains trusted in Edge may fail validation in other browsers. This fragmentation forces CAs to maintain multiple root strategies and complicates incident response when store policies diverge.
intros.conc: The market HHI of 2189 signals moderate concentration with systemic dependency risks concentrated in the top three providers who control 74% of issuance. A failure at Internet Security Research Group or Google Trust Services would impact over half of all TLS certificates, yet these high-volume CAs show the same trust store privileges as operators issuing a fraction of 1% of certificates. The 91% top-five share creates a two-tier ecosystem where a handful of providers operate at internet scale while dozens maintain full trust with minimal validation volume.
intros.tail: Seventy-five CAs each hold less than 0.1% market share yet maintain full inclusion across major trust stores, creating asymmetric risk exposure. These low-volume operators receive identical trust privileges to high-volume providers despite processing orders of magnitude fewer certificate requests, limiting their operational experience with edge cases and incident response. The 1596 total incidents across 54 CAs demonstrate that trust store inclusion does not correlate with issuance volume, leaving relying parties exposed to CAs with limited production validation.
intros.geo: United States-incorporated CAs issue 93% of all certificates despite representing only 15 of 89 trusted CAs, while 44 European CAs collectively issue 7% and 17 Asia-Pacific CAs contribute 0.1%. This geographic concentration means the global WebPKI depends overwhelmingly on entities subject to US corporate law and jurisdiction, regardless of where certificate subscribers or relying parties are located. The European long tail of 44 CAs with minimal issuance creates governance overhead without meaningfully diversifying the trust base.
intros.gov: Thirty government-operated or state-owned CAs hold trust store positions but collectively issue only 0.08% of certificates, indicating their inclusion serves policy goals beyond market demand. These CAs often appear on jurisdiction risk lists for compelled disclosure or lawful interception requirements, yet maintain the same technical trust as commercial providers. The combination of state control and full trust privileges creates a vector for surveillance or misissuance that the 93% US market concentration does not address.
intros.jurisdiction: Five high-risk jurisdictions maintain trusted CAs despite legal frameworks requiring compelled disclosure, lawful interception, or extraterritorial data access: China, Russia, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong. India and Turkey present moderate risk with expanding surveillance authorities. These jurisdiction risks compound the government CA findings, as 30 state-operated CAs may face legal obligations to compromise certificate integrity or disclose private keys under national security demands.
intros.ops: CAs have disclosed 1596 incidents across 54 organizations, with misissuance accounting for 617 events and governance failures contributing 513 cases. Only 27% of incidents are self-detected, while 8% emerge from audits and 18% from external researchers, indicating systemic surveillance gaps. Policy failures account for 200 incidents and disclosure failures for 143, suggesting the 6657-obligation regulatory surface does not prevent operational breakdowns at the same CAs holding trust for 91% of issuance volume.
intros.crypto: Root certificate cryptographic posture shows ongoing migration from SHA-1 and 2048-bit RSA to SHA-256 and higher key sizes, though legacy roots remain trusted to support older certificate chains. The 335 roots across trust stores include algorithms and key sizes that no longer meet current standards, maintained for backward compatibility despite known weaknesses. This technical debt intersects with the 142 Microsoft-only roots that may lag cryptographic modernization efforts visible in Chrome and Mozilla.
intros.distrust: Sixteen distrust events have removed or restricted CA trust since formal tracking began, with 14 attributed to compliance and operations failures rather than technical compromise. Seven cases involved negligent noncompliance, three demonstrated incompetence, and three indicated willful circumvention of requirements. The median 1185-day runway from distrust announcement to enforcement shows root programs balance ecosystem stability against incident severity, though the pattern-of-issues trigger appears in 10 of 16 events.
intros.policy: Certificate lifespans face three-phase reduction under SC-081: 200 days maximum in March 2026, 100 days in March 2027, and 47 days in March 2029, yet only 8 of 36 active TLS CAs currently issue certificates at the final 47-day threshold. Five CAs remain at risk of non-compliance even with the 100-day 2027 requirement based on median validity periods of 69 days, while the regulatory surface has expanded 121-fold since 2000 to 6657 total obligations with zero new ballots since 2022. The compliance burden grows even as CAs struggle to adapt issuance practices to shorter validity periods, with 76% of obligations now mandatory rather than recommended.
intros.governance: Root program oversight coverage has collapsed from 68% Chrome and 78% Mozilla participation in 2019 incidents to 18% Chrome and 10% Mozilla in 2025 across 223 total bugs. Microsoft provides zero substantive oversight comments across the 1884-bug corpus despite maintaining 142 exclusive roots not trusted by other stores. Chrome has filed substantive comments on 293 bugs historically with 112 recent, while Mozilla shows 249 substantive across 819 oversight bugs but only 47 recent, indicating declining engagement as the 6657-obligation regulatory surface expands.
intros.community: The CA/Browser Forum includes 56 member organizations but only 21 actively contribute to policy development, leaving 35 members with zero ballot participation. Sectigo leads organizational contribution while Stephen Davidson has proposed 36 ballots individually, concentrating policy authority in a small group. This participation gap means CAs holding trust for 91% of issuance may operate under requirements shaped by the active minority, while the silent majority consumes the 121-fold expanded regulatory surface without shaping its evolution.
intros.audit: Auditors detected only 33% of the 426 in-scope incidents that occurred during their audit periods, allowing 286 compliance failures to persist despite clean WebTrust and ETSI opinions. Thirty-nine CAs show high transparency gaps between audit letter assertions and Bugzilla incident histories, while five qualified opinions and 10 ETSI v3.5 reports under the new standard indicate emerging disclosure. Nine CAs changed auditors in 2025, and self-reported findings appear in 60% of WebTrust and 67% of ETSI letters, suggesting the 27% self-detection rate in operational incidents does not translate to proactive audit disclosure.
